reports.summary: I read the playbook in full, took the remediation diff (0b77fbe..HEAD over controllers/pkg/cmd/api/internal/test/hack/e2e, 22 files, +1096/-55), and hunted playbook class 3 by execution rather than by reading. I copied the tree to /tmp/jt (no repo file was created, edited, or deleted) and wrote four probes: two metamorphic order-invariance probes over the exact scenarios the change exercises (pkg/resolver reclaim/lottery with the new "\x00unbound-namespace/<ns>" bucket key under all 24 permutations of in.Leases plus 400 identical-input rounds to catch Go map randomization; controllers ActivateReservations+Reconcile over a CONFLICTED namespace with an unfunded RUNNING neighbour and a well-bound foreign tenant, 24 lease permutations plus 200 identical-input rounds with three competing terminal failures), and two behavioural probes. Both order-invariance probes PASS: the resolver verdict and the engine outcome (run phase/message/width/conditions, lease closure+reason, reservation state/countdown/reason, pod plane, and the joined error text) are byte-identical under every ordering. The probes were validated as not decorative by mutation: deleting sortTokensByOwner turns both resolver probes red immediately. deriveOwners' sorted walk plus its lexicographic-min fold is genuinely commutative, and the resolver's ownerOf change (NUL-prefixed key) introduces no ordering dependence, because owners are uniqued+sorted and tokens are sorted before the seeded draw. So the answer to the literal shuffle question is: INVARIANT. But the hunt found a real last-writer-wins defect one level up, between engine entry points rather than inside a loop: run.Status.Message for a namespace with no funding principal has two disagreeing writers, and the durable winner is the wrong one. The new guard at run_controller.go:1217 writes the informative "no funding principal" message; Reconcile's admission arm at run_controller.go:400 writes cover.PlanError's "owner and flavor must be set" - the exact string the change's own test asserts must never be shown. Because ReservationReconciler returns early once the reservation is Failed while RunReconciler requeues the parked Pending run every 60s, the bad message is the permanent one. This was confirmed over 240 simulated hours and by mutation (deleting the guard's setState fails exactly one assertion in the entire repo, the transient one).

answers.question: 1. Find every assignment to run.Status.* (Phase, Message, Width, CheckpointDeadline) that happens INSIDE a loop in the changed code. For each, is the write guarded by a comparison against what is already there, or does the last iteration simply win?
answers.conclusion: The changed controllers code contains exactly two run.Status.* writes, both in the new guard in activateReservation (run_controller.go:1216-1226): setState(run, v1.RunStateUnfunded, ...) which writes Phase+Message+Conditions, and run.Status.Funding = summarizeRunFunding(run, ev). failReservationTerminally itself writes no run status (only Reservation.Status.State/CountdownSeconds and the backlog gauge). Both execute inside a loop transitively: ActivateReservations iterates `for _, key := range dueKeys` and calls activateReservation per reservation. NEITHER write is guarded by a comparison against what is already there - the last iteration simply wins. Within a single pass that is nevertheless safe, for two reasons checked rather than assumed: dueKeys is sorted (run_controller.go:1057) so the iteration order is a specification, and if two reservations of the SAME run both reach the guard they compute a byte-identical message from run.Namespace alone, so the fold is idempotent. The 200-round map-iteration probe with three competing terminal failures in one namespace confirmed the state and the joined error text are stable. Neither Width nor CheckpointDeadline is written by the new block (a minor gap: sibling terminal branches refresh run.Status.Width, so a run that had a stale Width keeps it - not an ordering issue, so it was not raised as a finding). The unguarded write that actually bites is not inside the loop at all: it is the same field written by a SECOND engine entry point with a different value; see finding 1.

answers.question: 2. Find every `for k := range someMap` in the changed code. Go randomizes map iteration order per process. Does any observable outcome depend on that order?
answers.conclusion: Three map ranges survive in the changed code, all in pkg/funding/evaluate.go's deriveOwners, and the change converted two others to sortedKeys. (a) evaluate.go:244 `for ns := range nss` is still a raw map range, but its body is now a commutative min-fold (`if prior, ok := collided[ns]; !ok || owner < prior`, evaluate.go:245-247), so the result is order-independent by construction - the correct shape. (b) evaluate.go:268 `for owner := range owners` is a raw map range performing an UNGUARDED write, ev.ownerByNamespace[ns] = owner. It is safe today only because the `len(owners) >= 2 { ...; continue }` branch immediately above guarantees the map has exactly one element; that is a guard making a last-writer-wins loop harmless, not a fold, and it silently becomes a coin flip if the multiple-owner fail-safe is ever relaxed or scoped. Worth a one-line `for owner := range owners { ... break }` -> direct single-key read, or an explicit comment. (c) evaluate.go:238 and :254 are the two the change fixed: they now walk sortedKeys(nsByOwner)/sortedKeys(ownersByNS). No new map range appears in controllers/run_controller.go, pkg/resolver/resolver.go, or cmd/scheduler/plugin/gang.go (gang.go's loop is `for i := range budgetList.Items`, a slice, and funding.OwnerOfNamespace is fed a cluster-scoped, unfiltered List so it sees the same budget set the engine does). Executed answer: no observable outcome depends on map order. 400 identical-input rounds in pkg/resolver, 200 in controllers, and the repo's own 200-round funding test all produced byte-identical results.

answers.question: 3. Apply the metamorphic test: take a scenario the change exercises, SHUFFLE the order of state.Leases, replay, and compare the resulting run statuses and lease closure reasons byte-for-byte. Report whether the outcome is invariant. Run it several times. This is the definitive experiment — actually run it.
answers.conclusion: Ran, twice over, in two packages. (A) pkg/resolver: four unfunded runs across two CONFLICTED namespaces (the exact shape the new "\x00unbound-namespace/<ns>" bucket key exists for), Deficit=8, fixed SeedSource, all 24 permutations of in.Leases; the action list is identical both as an ordered sequence and as a set. A companion probe replayed identical input 400 times in one process across three conflicted namespaces (9 runs) and got the same three victims every round. (B) controllers: namespace `default` conflicted by a second-owner Budget, holding a Pending run with a due reservation (the new terminal path), a RUNNING neighbour on two open leases that the same conflict just reclassified Unfunded, and a well-bound tenant in another namespace; six simulated ticks of Reconcile (over SORTED run keys, so the harness is not the source of order) plus ActivateReservations, all 24 permutations of state.Leases, fingerprinting run phase/message/width/conditions, every lease's closed+ClosureReason, every reservation's state/reason/countdown, and the pod plane. Byte-identical in every permutation, and stable across 200 identical-input rounds including the joined error text of three simultaneous terminal failures. So: INVARIANT. Critically, the probes were proven able to see a violation before trusting the pass - commenting out the two sortTokensByOwner calls made both resolver probes fail on round 1 with a different victim, so the green is evidence and not silence. Both fixtures also survived pkg/invariant, which panicked on the first controllers fixture (INV-LEASE-HAS-POD) and forced the state to be made legal before it would run at all.

answers.question: 4. If an ordering dependence exists, is the correct fix a deterministic sort, or a COMMUTATIVE fold (a severity lattice, a post-loop sweep)? Argue for one. A deterministic order that happens to give the right answer is still a coincidence.
answers.conclusion: Two separate answers, because the change contains two situations. (i) For deriveOwners the shipped fix is both a sort AND a fold, and the fold is the load-bearing half: sorting nsByOwner alone would only have made the coin flip repeatable, whereas `!ok || owner < prior` makes the answer independent of any traversal. That is right, and the sort is then merely cosmetic ordering of the emitted Conflicts slice. It would be worth going one step further and making the fold lossless rather than min-selecting (see finding 2): the min is deterministic but still discards the second culprit. (ii) For the defect actually found, NEITHER is available, and that is the point. The two writers of run.Status.Message live in two different controllers - RunReconciler (reconcilers.go:126) and ReservationReconciler (reconcilers.go:378) - driven by independent watch/requeue triggers under the bridge mutex. There is no single loop to sort and no single pass to sweep; "deterministic order" is not a thing that exists between two Kubernetes controllers. A severity lattice on Message would also be wrong: the two strings are not two severities of one condition, they are one condition described correctly and incorrectly. The correct fix is the class-2 shape the playbook prescribes for failRun: make the value a pure function of state so that WHICHEVER writer runs last computes the same string. Concretely, hoist the empty-owner test out of activateReservation into a helper and apply it in Reconcile before building the cover.Request, so run_controller.go:400's InvalidRequest arm can never be reached with an empty owner. Then order stops mattering by construction, which is strictly stronger than any ordering discipline and is the only fix that survives someone adding a third writer.

findings.failure_scenario: An admin adds a second-owner Budget to a namespace holding a Pending run with a due reservation. Tick 1: ActivateReservations fails the reservation terminally and writes the good message (run_controller.go:1217, "namespace %q has no funding principal ..."). From then on ReservationReconciler never calls ActivateReservations for that reservation again (controllers/kube/reconcilers.go:368 returns early once State != "Pending"), while the run is parked Pending with PendingReservation == nil, so RunReconciler requeues it every pendingRunResync (60s) and rewrites the message via the admission arm at run_controller.go:400 to cover.PlanError's "owner and flavor must be set" - literally the string the change's own comment says must never be shown. Within 60 seconds of the fix firing, the operator-facing half of the fix is gone permanently, and the run's only pointer to the real diagnosis (the Failed reservation's Reason) is unreachable from the run because PendingReservation is nil. Confirmed via mutation: deleting the guard's setState line fails exactly one assertion in the whole repository, controllers/tenancy_reservation_test.go:96, which asserts the message only in the single instant it holds, on a state where Reconcile has never run afterward - i.e. the test certifies a 60-second transient as if it were the steady state.

findings.title: deriveOwners' collision fold is deterministic but lossy: a namespace poisoned by two spanning leaf owners reports only the lexicographically smallest
findings.failure_scenario: Namespace `shared` is bound by org:x (also in x-only) and org:y (also in y-only). The diagnostic names org:x because of the min-fold at evaluate.go:245 (`if prior, ok := collided[ns]; !ok || owner < prior`), and BindingConflict carries a single Owner field so org:y is never surfaced; also the `collided` branch `continue`s before the len(owners) >= 2 test, so a namespace that is simultaneously multi-owner and leaf-spanning reports only ConflictLeafOwnerSpansNamespaces. An admin removes org:x's stray Budget, re-evaluates, and the namespace is STILL unbound, now blamed on org:y, with nothing having told them there were two problems in the first place; TestConflictDiagnosticsAreDeterministic only asserts stability of the rendering across 200 evaluations, never that both culprits appear, so this lossiness is untested and latent (the doc comment records Conflicts() has no production consumer yet) rather than live, but it is the exact shape of alarm that trains operators to distrust the alarm once it is wired to a consumer.

answers.question: Enumerate EVERY exit path (return, continue, break, panic, early error) of every function this change adds or modifies. For each, list which leases are open at that moment and which are closed. Name any path that exits with a lease open that should have been closed.
answers.conclusion: Eight functions are added or modified. (1) activateReservation gains ONE new exit, run_controller.go:1216-1225: it is reachable only after the `allocated := baseGangGPUsForRun(...) > 0` block has returned and after `runHasActivePods` returned false, so the run holds no open base-gang lease and no active pod; the only leases that can still be open for it are SPARE-role leases and Reason==Grow leases, both of which baseGangGPUsForRun skips (run_controller.go:2811-2815). It closes nothing and sets the RUN to RunStateUnfunded (= RunPhasePending, api/v1/conditions.go:133), so the run never becomes terminal and SettleLeases never sees it. I executed the spare case (spare lease + spare pod + conflicted namespace, 20 ticks / 20 h): the spare stays open — but it stays open identically at 0b77fbe and identically in a healthy namespace, and settle.go's rule (1) explicitly refutes 'spare with no active lease is an orphan' as a legal state, so I do not charge it to this change. (2) failReservationNoEnvelope now has exactly one exit, delegating; both of its call sites (1357, 1378) sit under the same allocated==0 gate, so same lease picture. (3) failReservationTerminally (new) has one exit, closes nothing, and touches no lease. (4) promiseProvenanceValid gains a new `return false` at gang.go:756 — this is the one exit in the whole diff with a lease consequence, because refusing at PreBind means the pod never binds while its already-minted SIBLING leases stay open (see finding 1). (5) deriveOwners: same two exits, loops now ordered. (6) OwnerOfNamespace (new): one exit, no leases. (7) ownerOf: two exits, both pure map/sort keys, no leases. (8) sortedKeys: generic-ised, one nil-return for empty, no leases. The path that exits with a lease open that should have been closed is (4) — indirectly, by making the rest of a gang unmintable while its minted members hold GPUs forever.

answers.question: Does the change add a new CALLER to an existing function whose lease-closing behaviour was only correct for its old callers? failRun once carried the comment "It never holds leases at this point" — true when written, falsified by a new caller. Check every function the diff newly calls.
answers.conclusion: The newly-called functions are: funding.OwnerOfNamespace (new, called from promiseProvenanceValid), failReservationTerminally (new, called from activateReservation:1222 and failReservationNoEnvelope:1508), Evaluation.OwnerOf (newly called conditionally from resolver.ownerOf), and sortedKeys (newly called on ownersByNS/nsByOwner). None of these closes leases, so none has a closure contract to falsify — failRun, releaseRun, completeRun, closeRunLeases and CloseLease are untouched by the diff and gain no new caller. The real instance of this pattern here is the INVERSE and is worse: the diff adds a new REFUSAL to an existing function on the sole-committer path (promiseProvenanceValid, gang.go:755-757), whose old behaviour was correct only because it ACCEPTED conflicted namespaces. PreBind translates false into fwk.Error, so the new caller-visible behaviour is 'this pod never mints', and the pre-existing assumption that every emitted Promise pod eventually mints — which is what makes topUpActiveGang's re-emission loop converge and what makes a partially-minted gang's open leases temporary — is now false. I verified the reversal by execution against the base tree: promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted) is true at 0b77fbe and false at HEAD.

answers.question: Does the change set a run to a terminal phase (Failed / Completed) anywhere? For each such site, prove that every lease referencing that run is closed on the same path or by a sweep that provably runs. Cite the sweep.
answers.conclusion: No. The only production run-phase write the diff adds is `setState(run, v1.RunStateUnfunded, ...)` at run_controller.go:1217, and RunStateUnfunded is declared with `Phase: RunPhasePending` (api/v1/conditions.go:133), so the run stays non-terminal. What goes terminal is the RESERVATION (`reservation.Status.State = "Failed"`, run_controller.go:1522), which owns no leases. That means no lease-closure obligation is created by the diff — but it also means the repo's one self-healing sweep is structurally unable to help: SettleLeases 'retires every TERMINAL run' (controllers/settle.go:103) and skips any lease whose run is not Failed/Complete (`if !terminal[key] { continue }`, settle.go:133). I executed SettleLeases against both wedged states from finding 1 and it returned an empty sweep both times, because the run sits at RunPhasePending. So for the leases stranded by the new PreBind refusal there is NO sweep that provably runs, and no timeout anywhere fails an assembling run (the plugin's gangTTL sweep only drops the in-memory gang commit, gang.go:610-620).

answers.question: Does the change write Lease.Status.Closed anywhere other than closeLease()? Every clone of the closing obligation drifts. Name each site and say what closeLease does that the clone does not (events, metrics, ClosureReason).
answers.conclusion: No. Grepping every added line of `git diff 0b77fbe..HEAD -- controllers pkg cmd api internal test hack/e2e` for `Closed` or `CloseLease` returns zero hits, so controllers.CloseLease remains the sole closer and hack/antifake/soleclose.go still has nothing to catch. The cloned obligation the diff DOES leave live is one level up, on reservations: failReservationTerminally (run_controller.go:1521) is documented as 'the one transition every permanently-unfundable reservation makes', yet activateReservation's run-not-found branch performs the same three steps inline at run_controller.go:1107-1109 and was not refactored onto it. Today the clone matches step for step (State=Failed, CountdownSeconds=nil, ClearReservationBacklog), so nothing has drifted yet; the divergence risk is the standard one — the helper's next step (an Event, a Reason, a metric) will not happen on the run-not-found path — plus a latent key mismatch, since the clone clears the gauge under the caller's map key while the helper reconstructs keys.NamespacedKey(reservation.Namespace, reservation.Name).

answers.question: Take the single most suspicious path you found. Write a Go test that reaches it, drive Reconcile ~20 times over ~20 simulated hours, and assert the lease is closed. Report the actual test output. If it stays open you have a critical finding; if it closes, say what closed it and cite that code.
answers.conclusion: IT STAYS OPEN — critical. I wrote the tests in a copy of the tree at /tmp/lensA (never in the repo) and the base at /tmp/lensB. Two variants of the most suspicious path, both driving 20 Reconciles over 20 simulated hours plus ActivateReservations, plus an explicit SettleLeases at the end. (A) /tmp/lensA/controllers/zz_lensa_partial_test.go, TestLensAPartialPromiseGangInConflictedNamespace: 't0: OwnerOf(default)="" baseGang=2 open=[gang-lease-a gang-lease-b]' ... 'final: phase=Pending msg="assembling gang: 2/4 GPUs held (awaiting the jobtree scheduler)" openLeases=[gang-lease-a gang-lease-b] pods=4 sweep=[]' ... GPUs:map[Unfunded:3] GPUHours:map[Unfunded:63.083333333333336]'. Both bound-namespace controls PASS at RunPhaseRunning. Supporting probes: TestLensATopUpPodIsAPromisePod shows the re-emitted rank carries lease-reason="Promise" with payer org:ai:team/team/west, so PreBind routes it through promiseProvenanceValid and not the ordinary funding gate; and in /tmp/lensB (0b77fbe) TestLensBBasePromiseInConflictedNamespace logs 'BASE promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted namespace) = true' / '(unbound namespace) = false', which pins the regression to the conflicted case introduced at cmd/scheduler/plugin/gang.go:755-757. Nothing closed the leases: SettleLeases skipped them at controllers/settle.go:133 because the run is RunPhasePending, and the full test suite for controllers, controllers/kube, pkg/funding, pkg/resolver and cmd/scheduler/plugin is otherwise green — only my probes fail.

findings.title: New PreBind refusal for CONFLICTED namespaces strands a partial Promise gang's already-minted leases open forever
findings.failure_scenario: Executed. (a) Partial promise gang: 4-GPU Promise gang, 2 of 4 ranks minted, admin adds a second-owner Budget to the namespace. 20 Reconciles over 20 simulated hours -> open leases [gang-lease-a gang-lease-b], phase=Pending, msg="assembling gang: 2/4 GPUs held", SettleLeases sweep=[] , funding account GPUs:map[Unfunded:2] GPUHours:map[Unfunded:40.03333333333333]. (b) Live gang: 4/4 Promise gang Running, node failure closes rank 3's lease and removes its pod, admin adds the second Budget. topUpActiveGang re-emits rank 3 (verified: lease-reason="Promise", payer org:ai:team/team/west), PreBind refuses it. After 20 hours -> open leases [gang-lease-a gang-lease-b gang-lease-c], phase=Pending, sweep=[], GPUHours:map[Unfunded:63.083333333333336]. Both bound-namespace controls reach RunPhaseRunning. Attribution proved on the base tree: at 0b77fbe `promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted namespace) = true`, `promiseProvenanceValid(unbound namespace) = false`; at HEAD the shipped TestPromiseProvenanceRefusedWhenNamespaceConflicted asserts false. So the conflicted case, and only the conflicted case, is newly refused — and the refusal converts a bounded Unfunded occupancy (gang assembles, runs, completeRun closes every lease) into an unbounded one. Nothing goes red: the full suite passes and the invariant oracle is silent because the run is Pending, not terminal, so neither INV terminal-cleanliness nor INV-WIDTH-ASSEMBLED applies. This is exactly the reaping property the 2026-07-25 consequence seat used to veto the seg.Owner pin ('would wedge a healthy, funded, RUNNING gang forever on PreBind refusal'), reintroduced by the sibling check that stayed, under a MORE ordinary admin action (adding a Budget rather than renaming an owner).

The test therefore proves nothing about recovery. A real assertion exists and is cheap: my probe shows the repaired run reaches phase=Pending with msg="scheduling 4 GPUs (awaiting the jobtree scheduler)" and 4 emitted active pods, none of which the unrepaired run ever produces.

Investigator reviewed the diff 0b77fbe..HEAD (working tree at 2666bd0, two commits past the pinned ec5cb64) through the immortal-lease and cloned-obligation lenses using executed differential probes against a copy of the tree (/tmp/lensA) and a git-archive extraction of the base commit (/tmp/lensB), rather than static reading alone. The controller-side reservation fix (activateReservation's new empty-owner branch) is judged clean: it is gated on baseGangGPUsForRun==0 and !runHasActivePods, sets the run to RunStateUnfunded (RunPhasePending, non-terminal), and writes Lease.Status.Closed nowhere, leaving the sole-closer rail untouched. Investigator reviewed the R7-pt2 remediation diff (0b77fbe..HEAD, 22 files, +1096/-55) across controllers, pkg, cmd, api, internal, test, hack/e2e, using SIGNAL != REALITY, IDENTITY COARSENING, and GUARD BEFORE PREDICATE lenses. Work was done by copying the tree to /tmp/probe/repo (repo itself untouched) and writing nine executable probes against the pure engine and plugin fake-client manager; five hit. Headline finding (class 6): the new terminal guard at run_controller.go:1216 sits behind two earlier returns in the same function (allocated>0 at line 1122, runHasActivePods at line 1168), so the exact defect the fix was meant to kill -- an immortal Pending reservation with a lying/frozen or cleared backlog gauge -- survives via both bypass doors, confirmed by 20-tick executed probes. Class 4 finding: the change reads OBJECT ABSENCE (Budget existence/multiplicity) as a permanent fact with no debounce, and because ReservationReconciler polls every minute, an ordinary delete-then-apply or GitOps prune-then-apply window terminally Fails every due reservation cluster-wide. Sharper class-4 finding: Budget.Spec.Owner is a free-form string validated only for non-emptiness, with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that matches only pods, so a Budget created in ANY namespace naming another tenant's owner poisons that tenant via LeafOwnerSpansNamespaces, terminally kills its reservations, and makes PreBind refuse its own top-ups. Mutation-testing the new tests found that TestActivateReservationFailsTerminallyWhenNamespaceHasNoOwner's assertion doesn't survive a single Reconcile, because the unguarded sibling call site (run_controller.go:391-402) overwrites run.Status.Message with 'owner and flavor must be set', the exact string the test forbids -- passing only because the test never calls Reconcile. Additional findings: the seg.Owner pin removal (vetoed for wedging healthy running gangs) does not remove the underlying reaping mechanism, since the retained derived=="" refusal produces the identical outcome via gangProvenance rebuilding from the run's own open lease; baseGangGPUsForRun is coarser than 'any open lease matching runKey' since it skips Spare/Grow leases, letting a run with only such a lease open fall through to the terminal guard; and the interior-owner exemption in deriveOwners is keyed on owner string alone (continue before the span predicate), so it can be both weaponized and self-disabled via the same free-form field. Several hypotheses were cleared by probe or reading: EnvelopeKey correctly carries Namespace, OwnerOfNamespace is genuinely computed cluster-wide, the NUL bucket key never escapes pkg/resolver, and no production code compares errors by message text. The full existing test suite is reported green with all of these defects present.

answers.question: Does the change read any Kubernetes condition, taint, timestamp, or object-absence and treat it as a fact about what is PHYSICALLY running on a machine? For each: if that inference is wrong, WHAT RUNS TWICE?
answers.conclusion: No condition, taint or timestamp: grepping the whole reviewed diff for NodeReady, Unschedulable, Taint, LastTransitionTime and nodeUsable returns nothing, and the only Phase read added is `run.Status.Phase == RunPhaseFailed` in a test. The change DOES read object-absence, in two places, and treats it as permanent: `ev.OwnerOf(run.Namespace) == ""` (run_controller.go:1216) and `derived == ""` (gang.go:756) turn 'this namespace currently has no Budget, or has two owners' into 'this reservation can never activate' and 'this mint must be refused'. Nothing runs twice as a direct consequence -- both new refusals are fail-CLOSED, and PreBind returns its Error before the Lease is created, so there is no double-mint window. The harm runs the other way: work that should run does not, reservations are destroyed for conditions that lasted seconds (probe: one tick with zero Budgets = Failed), and leases are stranded open while the gang can never re-assemble. reports.summary: Investigator performed static analysis of a 22-file diff plus executed six probes against a pure engine (in /tmp, invariant oracle live) covering terminal-fail-then-repair recovery, conflicted-namespace scenarios with full/partial base gangs, an admission-path message leak, spare-only run behavior, and checkpoint-grace protection. The change adds a namespace-owner guard (activateReservation) and a derived-owner refusal (promiseProvenanceValid) plus removes a seg.Owner pin, without adding CloseLease calls or State.Pods writes, so no half-plane action is introduced. Two low-severity defects were confirmed: the 'owner and flavor must be set' operator message the fix intends to eliminate still surfaces and overwrites the new guard's message via Reconcile's admission path; and the recovery test (TestRunRecoversAfterTerminalFailureWhenBindingIsRepaired) passes even in a permanent-limbo scenario because its assertions don't discriminate real recovery from stuck-Pending-with-wrong-message. A third item, the assembling-hold door keeping a reservation Pending with a frozen backlog gauge during a permanent namespace conflict, was judged a non-defect (self-heals on repair, avoids reaping a mid-assembly gang). No new/incorrect invariant was found; the removed seg.Owner pin was verified safe by checking all Lease.Spec.Owner read sites. The change reduces eviction paths relative to before by placing the new guard prior to the resolver block.

The one grace shape that reaches the guard (all grace pods gone) has its reservation terminally failed but CheckpointDeadline is left untouched, and a conflicted namespace couldn't fund re-admission anyway. reports.summary: I reviewed the R7-pt2 remediation (0b77fbe..HEAD, 22 files, +1096/-55) exclusively through playbook class 8 -- does the test assert the bug -- and I answered every question by EXECUTING, not reading. I copied the repo to /tmp/scratch/jt (the repo itself was never modified; git status stayed clean throughout) and ran nine mutations plus nine probe tests. Baseline is green. Four mutations were correctly killed (the whole derived-owner guard in activateReservation; the CountdownSeconds clear in failReservationTerminally; the derived-owner refusal in gang.go; the ownerOf fallback in pkg/resolver, where the lottery probe measured 26/60 vs 11/60 pooled). Three mutations SURVIVED, and each is a real hole. (1) Deleting the admin repair from TestRunRecoversAfterTerminalFailureWhenBindingIsRepaired leaves it passing -- the test that is the sole evidence for the fixIsReaper=false ruling has an inert stimulus; a no-repair probe reaches phase=Pending with msg="owner and flavor must be set", satisfying both of its assertions. Worse, those two assertions read the PROCESS-GLOBAL metrics map with len(backlog) != 0, so on the pristine tree `go test ./controllers/ -shuffle=on` fails 4 runs in 5 with other tests' reservations in the map. (3) Neutering the post-applyResolution failReservationNoEnvelope call site at run_controller.go:1357 to `return nil` leaves ./controllers/... green -- the claim that this function "finally has tests" covers only the 1378 site. reports.summary: Investigator report for class-3 LAST-WRITER-WINS lens on commit ec5cb64, examining the tenancy/reservation remediation diff (0b77fbe..HEAD over controllers/pkg/cmd/api/internal/test/hack/e2e, 22 files, +1096/-55). The investigator copied the tree to /tmp/jt and wrote four probes: two metamorphic order-invariance probes over pkg/resolver reclaim/lottery and controllers ActivateReservations+Reconcile scenarios (24 lease permutations plus 400/200 identical-input rounds), and two behavioural probes. Both order-invariance probes PASS: resolver verdict and engine outcome are byte-identical under every ordering, validated as non-decorative by mutation (deleting sortTokensByOwner turns both resolver probes red immediately). So the literal shuffle question answer is INVARIANT. However, the hunt found a real last-writer-wins defect one level up, between engine entry points rather than inside a loop: run.Status.Message for a namespace with no funding principal has two disagreeing writers, and the durable winner is the wrong one. The new guard at run_controller.go:1217 writes the informative "no funding principal" message; Reconcile's admission arm at run_controller.go:400 writes cover.PlanError's "owner and flavor must be set" - the exact string the change's own test asserts must never be shown. Because ReservationReconciler returns early once the reservation is Failed while RunReconciler requeues the parked Pending run every 60s, the bad message is the permanent one. This was confirmed over 240 simulated hours and by mutation (deleting the guard's setState fails exactly one assertion in the entire repo, the transient one). A second, lower-severity finding concerns deriveOwners' collision fold in pkg/funding/evaluate.go: it is deterministic (correctly fixing the original coin-flip) but lossy, reporting only the lexicographically smallest of possibly multiple colliding owners.

answers.question: Find every assignment to run.Status.* (Phase, Message, Width, CheckpointDeadline) that happens INSIDE a loop in the changed code. For each, is the write guarded by a comparison against what is already there, or does the last iteration simply win?
answers.conclusion: The changed controllers code contains exactly two run.Status.* writes, both in the new guard in activateReservation (run_controller.go:1216-1226): setState(run, v1.RunStateUnfunded, ...) which writes Phase+Message+Conditions, and run.Status.Funding = summarizeRunFunding(run, ev). Both execute inside a loop transitively via ActivateReservations' `for _, key := range dueKeys`. NEITHER write is guarded by a comparison against what is already there - the last iteration simply wins. Within a single pass this is safe because dueKeys is sorted and same-run reservations compute a byte-identical message from run.Namespace alone (confirmed by a 200-round map-iteration probe). Neither Width nor CheckpointDeadline is written by the new block. The unguarded write that actually bites is not inside the loop at all: it is the same field written by a SECOND engine entry point with a different value; see finding 1.

answers.question: Find every `for k := range someMap` in the changed code. Go randomizes map iteration order per process. Does any observable outcome depend on that order?
answers.conclusion: Three map ranges survive in the changed code, all in pkg/funding/evaluate.go's deriveOwners, and the change converted two others to sortedKeys. (a) evaluate.go:244 `for ns := range nss` is a raw map range but its body is now a commutative min-fold, order-independent by construction. (b) evaluate.go:268 `for owner := range owners` is a raw map range performing an unguarded write, ev.ownerByNamespace[ns] = owner, safe today only because a preceding len(owners) >= 2 branch guarantees the map has exactly one element - a guard making a last-writer-wins loop harmless, not a fold, and it silently becomes a coin flip if that fail-safe is ever relaxed. (c) evaluate.go:238 and :254 are the two the change fixed, now walking sortedKeys. No new map range appears in controllers/run_controller.go, pkg/resolver/resolver.go, or cmd/scheduler/plugin/gang.go. Executed answer: no observable outcome depends on map order, confirmed via 400 identical-input rounds in pkg/resolver, 200 in controllers, and the repo's own 200-round funding test all producing byte-identical results.

answers.question: Apply the metamorphic test: take a scenario the change exercises, SHUFFLE the order of state.Leases, replay, and compare the resulting run statuses and lease closure reasons byte-for-byte. Report whether the outcome is invariant. Run it several times. This is the definitive experiment — actually run it.
answers.conclusion: Ran, twice over, in two packages. (A) pkg/resolver: four unfunded runs across two CONFLICTED namespaces, Deficit=8, fixed SeedSource, all 24 permutations of in.Leases; the action list is identical both as an ordered sequence and as a set, and a companion probe replayed identical input 400 times across three conflicted namespaces with the same three victims every round. (B) controllers: a CONFLICTED namespace scenario with a Pending run, a due reservation, a RUNNING neighbour on two open leases, and a well-bound tenant elsewhere; six simulated ticks of Reconcile plus ActivateReservations, all 24 permutations of state.Leases, fingerprinting run phase/message/width/conditions, lease closure reasons, reservation state/reason/countdown, and the pod plane. Byte-identical in every permutation, stable across 200 identical-input rounds. Conclusion: INVARIANT. The investigator proved the probes could detect a violation before trusting the pass: commenting out the two sortTokensByOwner calls made both resolver probes fail on round 1 with a different victim.

answers.question: If an ordering dependence exists, is the correct fix a deterministic sort, or a COMMUTATIVE fold (a severity lattice, a post-loop sweep)? Argue for one. A deterministic order that happens to give the right answer is still a coincidence.
answers.conclusion: Two separate answers for two situations. (i) For deriveOwners the shipped fix is both a sort AND a fold, and the fold is the load-bearing half: sorting nsByOwner alone would only have made the coin flip repeatable, whereas the min-selecting fold makes the answer independent of any traversal; the sort is then merely cosmetic ordering of the emitted Conflicts slice. The investigator would go further and make the fold lossless rather than min-selecting (see finding 2). (ii) For the defect actually found, neither sort nor fold is available: the two writers of run.Status.Message live in two different controllers (RunReconciler at reconcilers.go:126 and ReservationReconciler at reconcilers.go:378) driven by independent watch/requeue triggers, so there is no single loop to sort and no single pass to sweep. A severity lattice on Message would also be wrong since the two strings are not two severities of one condition but one condition described correctly and incorrectly. The correct fix is to make the value a pure function of state so whichever writer runs last computes the same string - concretely, hoist the empty-owner test out of activateReservation into a helper applied in Reconcile before building the cover.Request, so run_controller.go:400's InvalidRequest arm can never be reached with an empty owner.

reports.summary: I reviewed 0b77fbe..HEAD (22 files, +1096/-55) through the immortal-lease (class 1) and cloned-obligation (class 7) lenses, and I did it by executing rather than reading: I copied the tree to /tmp/lensA, extracted 0b77fbe with `git archive` to /tmp/lensB, and ran differential probes against both. Note first that the working tree is at 2666bd0, TWO commits past the pinned ec5cb64 (42d9657 and 2666bd0); 2666bd0 rewrites two comment blocks in cmd/scheduler/plugin/gang.go and gang_test.go, shifting gang.go by +2 lines after line 768 — every citation below is at a line unaffected by that drift. On the controller side the fix is clean for my lens: the new empty-owner branch in activateReservation is gated behind `baseGangGPUsForRun == 0` and `!runHasActivePods`, it sets the RUN to RunStateUnfunded (which maps to RunPhasePending, not terminal), and the diff writes Lease.Status.Closed nowhere at all, so the sole-closer rail is untouched. The defect is on the PLUGIN side, and it is the playbook's own warning that 'a fix for this class can create this class'. The new `derived == ""` refusal in promiseProvenanceValid turns the SOLE COMMITTER from 'mints' into 'refuses forever' for a namespace that becomes CONFLICTED — and I proved the flip by execution: at 0b77fbe promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted) returns true, at HEAD it returns false (the unbound case was already false at base, so only the conflicted case is new). A Promise gang whose namespace goes conflicted mid-bind, or a live 4/4 Promise gang that loses one rank to a node failure afterwards, therefore keeps its already-minted leases OPEN forever: 20 Reconciles over 20 simulated hours left 2 and 3 open leases respectively, run stuck 'assembling gang: 2/4' / '3/4' at RunPhasePending, 40.0 and 63.1 Unfunded GPU-hours accrued, and SettleLeases — whose only rule is 'the run is Failed or Complete' — swept nothing. The bound-namespace controls recover to Running in both cases. I also mutated the new tests: TestRunRecoversAfterTerminalFailureWhenBindingIsRepaired PASSES with the admin repair deleted, because Reconcile overwrites the run message with cover's 'owner and flavor must be set' one tick later — which additionally defeats the operator-message half of the reservation fix. I investigated and then discarded the leftover-spare immortal-lease hypothesis: it reproduces identically at 0b77fbe and in a healthy namespace, and settle.go explicitly refutes that sweep rule as legal state.

answers.question: Enumerate EVERY exit path (return, continue, break, panic, early error) of every function this change adds or modifies. For each, list which leases are open at that moment and which are closed. Name any path that exits with a lease open that should have been closed.
answers.conclusion: Eight functions are added or modified. (1) activateReservation gains ONE new exit, run_controller.go:1216-1225: it is reachable only after the `allocated := baseGangGPUsForRun(...) > 0` block has returned and after `runHasActivePods` returned false, so the run holds no open base-gang lease and no active pod; the only leases that can still be open for it are SPARE-role leases and Reason==Grow leases, both of which baseGangGPUsForRun skips (run_controller.go:2811-2815). It closes nothing and sets the RUN to RunStateUnfunded (= RunPhasePending, api/v1/conditions.go:133), so the run never becomes terminal and SettleLeases never sees it. I executed the spare case (spare lease + spare pod + conflicted namespace, 20 ticks / 20 h): the spare stays open — but it stays open identically at 0b77fbe and identically in a healthy namespace, and settle.go's rule (1) explicitly refutes 'spare with no active lease is an orphan' as a legal state, so I do not charge it to this change. (2) failReservationNoEnvelope now has exactly one exit, delegating; both of its call sites (1357, 1378) sit under the same allocated==0 gate, so same lease picture. (3) failReservationTerminally (new) has one exit, closes nothing, and touches no lease. (4) promiseProvenanceValid gains a new `return false` at gang.go:756 — this is the one exit in the whole diff with a lease consequence, because refusing at PreBind means the pod never binds while its already-minted SIBLING leases stay open (see finding 1). (5) deriveOwners: same two exits, loops now ordered. (6) OwnerOfNamespace (new): one exit, no leases. (7) ownerOf: two exits, both pure map/sort keys, no leases. (8) sortedKeys: generic-ised, one nil-return for empty, no leases. The path that exits with a lease open that should have been closed is (4) — indirectly, by making the rest of a gang unmintable while its minted members hold GPUs forever.

answers.question: Does the change add a new CALLER to an existing function whose lease-closing behaviour was only correct for its old callers? failRun once carried the comment "It never holds leases at this point" — true when written, falsified by a new caller. Check every function the diff newly calls.
answers.conclusion: The newly-called functions are: funding.OwnerOfNamespace (new, called from promiseProvenanceValid), failReservationTerminally (new, called from activateReservation:1222 and failReservationNoEnvelope:1508), Evaluation.OwnerOf (newly called conditionally from resolver.ownerOf), and sortedKeys (newly called on ownersByNS/nsByOwner). None of these closes leases, so none has a closure contract to falsify — failRun, releaseRun, completeRun, closeRunLeases and CloseLease are untouched by the diff and gain no new caller. The real instance of this pattern here is the INVERSE and is worse: the diff adds a new REFUSAL to an existing function on the sole-committer path (promiseProvenanceValid, gang.go:755-757), whose old behaviour was correct only because it ACCEPTED conflicted namespaces. PreBind translates false into fwk.Error, so the new caller-visible behaviour is 'this pod never mints', and the pre-existing assumption that every emitted Promise pod eventually mints — which is what makes topUpActiveGang's re-emission loop converge and what makes a partially-minted gang's open leases temporary — is now false. I verified the reversal by execution against the base tree: promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted) is true at 0b77fbe and false at HEAD.

answers.question: Does the change set a run to a terminal phase (Failed / Completed) anywhere? For each such site, prove that every lease referencing that run is closed on the same path or by a sweep that provably runs. Cite the sweep.
answers.conclusion: No. The only production run-phase write the diff adds is `setState(run, v1.RunStateUnfunded, ...)` at run_controller.go:1217, and RunStateUnfunded is declared with `Phase: RunPhasePending` (api/v1/conditions.go:133), so the run stays non-terminal. What goes terminal is the RESERVATION (`reservation.Status.State = "Failed"`, run_controller.go:1522), which owns no leases. That means no lease-closure obligation is created by the diff — but it also means the repo's one self-healing sweep is structurally unable to help: SettleLeases 'retires every TERMINAL run' (controllers/settle.go:103) and skips any lease whose run is not Failed/Complete (`if !terminal[key] { continue }`, settle.go:133). I executed SettleLeases against both wedged states from finding 1 and it returned an empty sweep both times, because the run sits at RunPhasePending. So for the leases stranded by the new PreBind refusal there is NO sweep that provably runs, and no timeout anywhere fails an assembling run (the plugin's gangTTL sweep only drops the in-memory gang commit, gang.go:610-620).

answers.question: Does the change write Lease.Status.Closed anywhere other than closeLease()? Every clone of the closing obligation drifts. Name each site and say what closeLease does that the clone does not (events, metrics, ClosureReason).
answers.conclusion: No. Grepping every added line of `git diff 0b77fbe..HEAD -- controllers pkg cmd api internal test hack/e2e` for `Closed` or `CloseLease` returns zero hits, so controllers.CloseLease remains the sole closer and hack/antifake/soleclose.go still has nothing to catch. The cloned obligation the diff DOES leave live is one level up, on reservations: failReservationTerminally (run_controller.go:1521) is documented as 'the one transition every permanently-unfundable reservation makes', yet activateReservation's run-not-found branch performs the same three steps inline at run_controller.go:1107-1109 and was not refactored onto it. Today the clone matches step for step (State=Failed, CountdownSeconds=nil, ClearReservationBacklog), so nothing has drifted yet; the divergence risk is the standard one — the helper's next step (an Event, a Reason, a metric) will not happen on the run-not-found path — plus a latent key mismatch, since the clone clears the gauge under the caller's map key while the helper reconstructs keys.NamespacedKey(reservation.Namespace, reservation.Name).

Report the actual test output. If it stays open you have a critical finding; if it closes, say what closed it and cite that code.

'final: phase=Pending msg="assembling gang: 2/4 GPUs held (awaiting the jobtree scheduler)" openLeases=[gang-lease-a gang-lease-b] pods=4 sweep=[]' ... findings.title: New PreBind refusal for CONFLICTED namespaces strands a partial Promise gang's already-minted leases open forever
findings.failure_scenario: Executed. (a) Partial promise gang: 4-GPU Promise gang, 2 of 4 ranks minted, admin adds a second-owner Budget to the namespace. 20 Reconciles over 20 simulated hours -> open leases [gang-lease-a gang-lease-b], phase=Pending, msg="assembling gang: 2/4 GPUs held", SettleLeases sweep=[] , funding account GPUs:map[Unfunded:2] GPUHours:map[Unfunded:40.03333333333333]. (b) Live gang: 4/4 Promise gang Running, node failure closes rank 3's lease and removes its pod, admin adds the second Budget. topUpActiveGang re-emits rank 3 (verified: lease-reason="Promise", payer org:ai:team/team/west), PreBind refuses it. After 20 hours -> open leases [gang-lease-a gang-lease-b gang-lease-c], phase=Pending, sweep=[], GPUHours:map[Unfunded:63.083333333333336]. Both bound-namespace controls reach RunPhaseRunning. Attribution proved on the base tree: at 0b77fbe `promiseProvenanceValid(conflicted namespace) = true`, `promiseProvenanceValid(unbound namespace) = false`; at HEAD the shipped TestPromiseProvenanceRefusedWhenNamespaceConflicted asserts false. So the conflicted case, and only the conflicted case, is newly refused — and the refusal converts a bounded Unfunded occupancy (gang assembles, runs, completeRun closes every lease) into an unbounded one. Nothing goes red: the full suite passes and the invariant oracle is silent because the run is Pending, not terminal, so neither INV terminal-cleanliness nor INV-WIDTH-ASSEMBLED applies. This is exactly the reaping property the 2026-07-25 consequence seat used to veto the seg.Owner pin ('would wedge a healthy, funded, RUNNING gang forever on PreBind refusal'), reintroduced by the sibling check that stayed, under a MORE ordinary admin action (adding a Budget rather than renaming an owner).

reports.summary: Investigator reviewed the R7-pt2 remediation diff (0b77fbe..HEAD, controllers/pkg/cmd/api/internal/test/hack-e2e, 22 files +1096/-55) using SIGNAL != REALITY, IDENTITY COARSENING and GUARD BEFORE PREDICATE lenses, verifying hypotheses by copying the repo to /tmp/probe and running nine executable probes against the pure engine and the plugin's fake-client manager (five hit). The two headline results are class-6 GUARD BEFORE PREDICATE: the new terminal guard at run_controller.go:1216 sits behind two earlier returns (lines 1122 and 1168) in the same function, so the exact defect the fix targeted -- an immortal Pending reservation with a frozen/lying backlog gauge -- survives on both paths, confirmed by 20-tick executed probes. A class-4 SIGNAL != REALITY finding treats object absence (no Budget, or conflicting owners) as a permanent fact with no debounce, so a routine delete-then-apply or GitOps prune window terminally Fails every due reservation cluster-wide within one poll (one minute). A related class-4/5 finding: Budget.Spec.Owner is a free-form string validated only for non-emptiness, unconstrained by RBAC or the shipped ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (which matches only pods), so a Budget in any namespace naming another tenant's owner poisons that tenant's namespace, terminally kills its reservations, and makes PreBind refuse its own top-ups. A mutation-testing finding shows the new test's assertion that the operator never sees 'owner and flavor must be set' is falsified by one ordinary Reconcile call at the unguarded sibling site (line 400), meaning the test passes only because it avoids calling the code path that breaks it. Two IDENTITY COARSENING findings show baseGangGPUsForRun skips Spare/Grow leases (letting a run reach the terminal guard with an open lease) and the interior-owner exemption in deriveOwners is keyed on owner string alone, self-serve to trigger or disable. Several hypotheses were cleared by probe or reading: EnvelopeKey correctly scopes by namespace, OwnerOfNamespace is computed cluster-wide consistently between engine and plugin, the NUL bucket key never escapes pkg/resolver, and no production code compares errors by message text. The full existing test suite is reported green with all of these defects present.

answers.question: Does the change read any Kubernetes condition, taint, timestamp, or object-absence and treat it as a fact about what is PHYSICALLY running on a machine? For each: if that inference is wrong, WHAT RUNS TWICE?
answers.conclusion: No condition, taint or timestamp: grepping the whole reviewed diff for NodeReady, Unschedulable, Taint, LastTransitionTime and nodeUsable returns nothing, and the only Phase read added is `run.Status.Phase == RunPhaseFailed` in a test. The change DOES read object-absence, in two places, and treats it as permanent: `ev.OwnerOf(run.Namespace) == ""` (run_controller.go:1216) and `derived == ""` (gang.go:756) turn 'this namespace currently has no Budget, or has two owners' into 'this reservation can never activate' and 'this mint must be refused'. Nothing runs twice as a direct consequence -- both new refusals are fail-CLOSED, and PreBind returns its Error before the Lease is created, so there is no double-mint window. The harm runs the other way: work that should run does not, reservations are destroyed for conditions that lasted seconds, and leases are stranded open while the gang can never re-assemble. There is one second-order physical consequence, and this diff's own new comment names it: the same misread reclassifies open leases Unfunded, and Unfunded is the resolver's FIRST reclaim target, so a mis-derived binding does eventually reach real container eviction -- just via the resolver rather than directly.

answers.question: For each such signal: WHO can write that field, and can they lie?
answers.conclusion: The signal is Budget.Spec.Owner, and yes, it can lie. api/v1/budget_types.go:188 validates it only for non-emptiness -- no format, no namespace scoping, no relationship to any authenticated identity. The shipped chart does not constrain it either: deploy/helm/gpu-fleet/templates/rbac.yaml defines only the controller ServiceAccount's ClusterRole and the scheduler-deployment.yaml ClusterRole gives the scheduler get/list/watch on runs, budgets, gpuleases -- neither says anything about who else may create a Budget, and the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy matches only `pods`, so no admission control sees a Budget at all. Because deriveOwners must run over every Budget cluster-wide to enforce injectivity, a lie is global: a Budget created in namespace `attacker` whose owner string is simply `org:team` flips OwnerOf("default") from "org:team" to "", emits LeafOwnerSpansNamespaces conflicts for both namespaces, terminally Fails default's reservation on the next tick, and makes the plugin refuse default's own top-up. The victim controls nothing in that chain.

answers.question: Does the change compare a COARSER key than the one that matters? Find every equality test on an identity and name the finest key that should have been used.
answers.conclusion: (1) `baseGangGPUsForRun(runKey, c.State.Leases) > 0` at run_controller.go:1122 skips Role==Spare and Reason==Grow (line 2811, 2814), so it is coarser than the property that matters, which is 'any open lease whose RunRef equals runKey'; a run holding only an open Grow lease reads 0 and falls through the guard with the lease open. (2) `interior[owner]` in deriveOwners keys on the owner string alone; the finest key is (owner, namespace), since an owner can be a pool in one namespace and a leaf in another -- P5, parked. (3) `ownerOf`'s NUL fallback in pkg/resolver is correct: both call sites use it only as a map key, a slice element and an rng index; it never reaches an Action, a Reason or a message. (4) EnvelopeKey is {Namespace, Budget, Envelope}, already the finest key, and the plugin's budget walk matches on b.Namespace + b.Name + env.Name, so the envelope-names-are-unique-only-within-a-Budget trap is not present. (5) funding.OwnerOfNamespace in the plugin derives from ALL budgets via a direct uncached client with no selectors, matching the engine's universe -- clear. (6) The reservation metric key is consistent across all writers of State.Reservations -- not a defect.

answers.question: Does the change contain a loop with BOTH a type/role filter (`if ... continue`) AND a match predicate? Check their ORDER.
answers.conclusion: Yes, one, and it is in the code the diff rewrote. deriveOwners' new sorted loop keeps `if _, isInterior := interior[owner]; isInterior { continue }` (evaluate.go:239) BEFORE the `if len(nss) >= 2` span predicate (line 243), so an owner that genuinely spans namespaces is suppressed before the test that decides it is a violation, no BindingConflict is recorded and no namespace is poisoned. The diff's own new TestInteriorExemptionAdmitsALeafOwnerInTwoNamespaces pins that hole rather than fixing it (P5, parked). The second loop is correctly ordered. The plugin's budget walk has a single combined match predicate and no role filter. No `handled`/`found` flag in the diff is left false on a path that handled something. The same class shows up at FUNCTION level rather than loop level and is the top finding: activateReservation's two early returns at lines 1122 and 1168 run before the predicate (line 1216) that decides the reservation can never activate, which is the R25 shape scaled up, and this was confirmed by execution.

answers.question: Grep the changed code and its callers for `strings.Contains(err.Error(), ...)` or any error compared by TEXT. Enumerate every error the changed functions can return and confirm each swallow site swallows only a typed sentinel via errors.Is.
answers.conclusion: No production code anywhere in the repo compares an error by text: grepping strings.Contains across controllers/ pkg/ cmd/ internal/ excluding _test.go returns zero hits, so this is clean on the shipped path. reports.summary: Investigator ran static analysis of a 22-file diff plus six executed probes against a pure engine with an invariant oracle live, in a scratch /tmp module (no repo files touched). Findings: no site closes a Lease while a pod still runs or deletes a Pod while a lease is open (the diff adds no CloseLease call and no State.Pods write). The checkpoint-grace window is protected by plane facts (open leases, active pods, deadline check) not phase names, and the guard does not reach it destructively. For each fix, the investigator names the legal state a more aggressive version would destroy (e.g. terminal guard one step further would kill a healthy adopted RUNNING gang; the seg.Owner pin removal's aggressive version would wedge a funded RUNNING gang at PreBind). No invariant was added or strengthened; two runtime refusals were added instead, and no probe panicked the invariant oracle. Two low-severity defects survived verification: (1) the 'owner and flavor must be set' operator message still surfaces and overwrites the new guard's message via Reconcile's admission path; (2) the recovery test cannot distinguish real recovery from permanent limbo because it only asserts phase != Failed and message doesn't contain a specific string. A third item is informational/non-defect: the assembling-hold door keeps a reservation Pending with a frozen backlog gauge during a permanent conflict, judged correct because it self-heals and bills nobody. Quantified cost: findings 1 and 2 hold zero GPUs and charge zero budget (diagnostic/test-coverage gaps only); finding 3 is informational, with GPUs held classed Unfunded (billing nobody) and self-healing on repair.

answers.question: For every site the change closes a Lease: whose container is still running? For every site it deletes a Pod: whose lease is still open? Name each pairing.
answers.conclusion: There are NO such sites: the diff adds no CloseLease call and no write to State.Pods anywhere. With an open base-gang lease the allocated>0 branch adopts and returns before the guard (probe 2); with active pods, line 1168 returns first (probe 5); with only a spare lease, the guard fires but touches neither plane, and after 20 simulated hours the spare lease and its pod are both still present together (probe 4), consistent, not half-plane. The new guard sits at 1216, before the resolver invocation at 1336, so a conflicted namespace terminally fails without evicting anyone.

answers.question: Does the change reach the checkpoint-grace window (a deliberate, bounded half-plane state)? Check the exemption keys on the deadline or on non-terminality, not on a phase name.
answers.conclusion: Executed (probe 5): a Pending run with CheckpointDeadline set, surviving active pods and no open lease, in a conflicted namespace, passes through ActivateReservations untouched. The protection keys on plane facts: open base-gang leases short-circuit at 1122, surviving containers short-circuit at runHasActivePods (1168), and grace expiry keys on CheckpointDeadline at Reconcile:228. The one grace shape that reaches the guard has its reservation terminally failed but CheckpointDeadline is untouched and grace semantics survive intact. Not a reaper.

answers.question: For each fix, state the legal state its repair would destroy if applied one step more aggressively.
answers.conclusion: (1) Terminal reservation guard: one step further (failing the RUN or closing its leases) would reap a conflicted-namespace run adopted to RUNNING with a full open base gang (probe 2), and a Failed run is never resurrected, so probe-1 recovery would be impossible. (2) seg.Owner pin removal: the aggressive version IS the pin, which would wedge a funded RUNNING gang at PreBind forever via a legacy owner string or admin Budget reorg; Evaluate never reads Lease.Spec.Owner so the pin bought nothing. (3) derived=="" refusal: extending it to SWAP pods would destroy node-failure recovery of a legally coasting gang. (4) resolver ownerOf NUL-key: excluding ownerless runs from buckets entirely would make conflicted-namespace work unreclaimable. (5) deriveOwners determinism: erroring/panicking on a multi-owner namespace would break a legal fail-safe admin state that must coast. (6) Fixture idle envelopes: forbidding binding-only Budgets would destroy the legal 'bound tier with no capacity of this flavor' shape.

answers.question: Does the change add or strengthen an INVARIANT? If so, find a legal state this engine really produces that would trip it.
answers.conclusion: The change adds nothing to pkg/invariant (no oracle entries, no panics). It adds two runtime refusals: the OwnerOf=="" guard in activateReservation and the derived=="" refusal in promiseProvenanceValid, plus pinned-behaviour tests. Legal states that trip the refusals were found (a stranded Promise pod when a namespace goes conflicted between emission and PreBind, a briefly-conflicted namespace killing a reservation object) but in each case they destroy only a status object, not funded work, since probe 1 proves self-recovery. All six probe states ran with the invariant oracle live and nothing panicked. No wrong invariant found.

answers.question: For each finding, which budget is charged, how many GPUs are held, and for how long?
answers.conclusion: Finding 1 (leftover operator message): zero GPUs held, zero budget charged; the harm is diagnostic and indefinite for as long as the namespace stays unbound/conflicted, costing operator time via a misleading message. Finding 2 (recovery test passes in limbo): zero direct charge and zero GPUs today since recovery is currently real (probe 1); exposure is only to a future regression that would strand a run at 0 GPUs until manual resubmission. reports.summary: I reviewed the R7-pt2 remediation (0b77fbe..HEAD, 22 files, +1096/-55) exclusively through playbook class 8 — does the test assert the bug — and I answered every question by EXECUTING, not reading. I copied the repo to /tmp/scratch/jt (the repo itself was never modified; git status stayed clean throughout) and ran nine mutations plus nine probe tests. Baseline is green. Four mutations were correctly killed (the whole derived-owner guard in activateReservation; the CountdownSeconds clear in failReservationTerminally; the derived-owner refusal in gang.go; the ownerOf fallback in pkg/resolver, where the lottery probe measured 26/60 vs 11/60 pooled). Three mutations SURVIVED, and each is a real hole. (1) Deleting the admin repair from TestRunRecoversAfterTerminalFailureWhenBindingIsRepaired leaves it passing — the test that is the sole evidence for the fixIsReaper=false ruling has an inert stimulus; a no-repair probe reaches phase=Pending with msg="owner and flavor must be set", satisfying both of its assertions. (2) Deleting metrics.ClearReservationBacklog from failReservationTerminally — the line its own doc comment calls "the part that is easy to forget" — leaves the entire ./controllers suite green, because both new fixtures set EarliestStart in the past so refreshReservationBacklog never arms the gauge; a probe that arms it legitimately (future EarliestStart, tick, then due) catches the mutant at 3600s and passes on real code. Worse, those two assertions read the PROCESS-GLOBAL metrics map with len(backlog) != 0, so on the pristine tree `go test ./controllers/ -shuffle=on` fails 4 runs in 5 with other tests' reservations in the map. (3) Neutering the post-applyResolution failReservationNoEnvelope call site at run_controller.go:1357 to `return nil` leaves ./controllers/... green — the claim that this function "finally has tests" covers only the 1378 site. I also found that two NEW fixtures build Budgets the API server rejects (no envelope Selector), in the very change that made fixture legality a rule and whose helper comment asserts legality; TestTenancyFixturesAreLegalBudgets validates hand-built copies in pkg/funding and structurally cannot see them. On Q5 the modified tests are sound: the gang_test.go assertion is identical to 0b77fbe (only comment/message changed) and re-adding the vetoed seg.Owner pin goes red, so the removal does have a rail; the idleEnvelope additions are pure legality repairs of a different flavor and change no measured outcome; the e2e webhook rewrite's new stimulus checks out, and narrowing IsForbidden||IsInvalid to IsForbidden is a strengthening.

answers.question: 2. Read each new assertion as a claim about the WORLD, not about the code. Is the asserted state actually DESIRABLE?
answers.conclusion: The core world-claim — a namespace with no funding principal can never activate a reservation, so fail it terminally — matches R7-tenancy-amendment.md §4 verbatim ("a *fresh* Run there cannot admit at all ... and the reservation path fails terminally"), so terminal IS the desirable state and the fix is right. But two assertions are world-claims the world falsifies. First, "the operator must not be told about fields the Run does not have" (asserted only against err.Error()): executing one ordinary Reconcile on the same conflicted state made run.Status.Message become exactly "owner and flavor must be set" — the operator-visible field the fix's own comment says it exists to avoid. Production runs two independent reconcilers (RunReconciler calls Reconcile, ReservationReconciler calls ActivateReservations), and the Pending run resyncs, so the good "no funding principal" message is overwritten on the very next tick. Second, "the backlog gauge must be cleared on the terminal path" is asserted as len(whole-global-map) == 0, which is a claim about every other test in the package rather than about this reservation. The R7 amendment's "coast Unfunded" wording and quota-semantics.md Decision 1 (unfunded is reclaimed first) are correctly reflected in the new evaluate.go doc comment, and the resolver's per-tenant bucket assertion is the right world-claim (one tenant, one ticket).
